segments.text: Friday, October sixteenth. Jakarta's trading screens turn red. <short pause> By the close, Indonesia's main index has fallen almost twelve percent. Its steepest one day drop since 1998.
Since January, the index has lost about forty percent.
The headlines name one culprit. <short pause> MSCI. The company whose indexes guide trillions of dollars of global investment.
It is weighing whether Indonesia should stay in its emerging markets index at all.
But the price data tells a longer story.
Rebase the big banks to the day before Prabowo took office. BCA is down almost half. Mandiri, a third. For more than a year, the index rose while the banks sank.
So this is not one bad week. <short pause> It is a slow leak that finally burst.
Three forces are worth checking. The index providers. The currency. <short pause> And the government.
Part one. Why an index provider matters.
MSCI groups countries into developed, emerging and frontier markets, based on size, openness and how easy it is for foreigners to trade.
Passive funds copy those indexes automatically. If a country's weight goes up, they buy. If it goes down, they sell, no matter what anyone thinks of the companies.
So a downgrade is not an opinion. <short pause> It is a sell order.
In January, MSCI paused all increases to Indonesia's weight.
Its concern was transparency. For many listed firms, it was hard to see who really controlled the shares.
Indonesian traders have a word for the worst of these stocks. <short pause> Gorengan. Fried food.
When only a small slice of a company trades, a few holders can move the price easily. Push it up, attract buyers, then sell into the rush.
After the freeze, the index fell about eight percent in two sessions.
Soon after, the heads of the stock exchange and of the financial regulator stepped down.
The response was a new floor. Listed companies must have at least fifteen percent of their shares in public hands, twice the old level.
It was a real reform. The question is whether it came in time. <short pause> And that is where the currency comes in.
